Transactions & Concurrency

88. Transactions

ACID Properties & Robustness

1. ACID Invariants & Engine Storage Mechanics

ACID PrincipleEngine GuaranteeUnderlying Storage Mechanism (InnoDB)
A - Atomicity"All or Nothing": Either every mutation commits to disk, or all modifications are rolled back.Undo Log: Records inverse operations (e.g. record insert logs a delete) to roll back uncommitted changes during failure.
C - ConsistencyData transitions strictly between valid schema states. Invariants (PK, FK, CHECK) are never violated.Constraint Checking & Doublewrite Buffer: Enforces database rules and prevents partial page writes.
I - IsolationConcurrent transactions cannot witness uncommitted state anomalies or interfere with each other.Lock Manager & MVCC: Shared/exclusive row locks and Read Views built from Undo Logs.
D - DurabilityOnce committed, updates survive power loss, hardware crashes, and OS reboots.Redo Log (Write-Ahead Logging / WAL): Changes are appended sequentially to disk before memory pages are flushed.

2. The 4 Concurrency Anomalies & Isolation Levels Matrix

When multiple database connections execute concurrently without total serialization, 4 distinct data corruption anomalies can occur:

ANSI Isolation LevelDirty ReadNon-Repeatable ReadPhantom ReadDefault In
READ UNCOMMITTEDYES (Dangerous)YESYESNever recommended
READ COMMITTEDPreventedYESYESPostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server
REPEATABLE READPreventedPreventedPrevented (via Next-Key Locks)MySQL (InnoDB Default)
SERIALIZABLEPreventedPreventedPreventedMaximum locking overhead

A Transaction is a sequence of one or more SQL statements executed as a single, indivisible unit of work. If all statements succeed, the changes are committed to the database. If any statement fails or is aborted, the entire transaction is rolled back, leaving the database in its original consistent state.

The ACID Properties:

  • Atomicity (All-or-Nothing): Either all statements succeed, or the entire transaction is completely undone.
  • Consistency: The database transitions from one valid state to another, strictly obeying all constraints and integrity rules.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions execute independently without interfering with one another.
  • Durability: Once committed, transaction results survive crashes, system reboots, and power outages.
Transactions & Concurrency

89. Creating Transactions

START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK

In MySQL, individual statements run with autocommit = 1 by default. To group statements into a single unit, use START TRANSACTION (or BEGIN), perform the operations, and finish with COMMIT to persist the changes or ROLLBACK to abort.

90. Concurrency and Locking

Row-Level Locks & Mutexes

Concurrency occurs when multiple users or application threads access the database simultaneously. To maintain consistency, MySQL uses Locking:

  • Exclusive Locks (X-Locks): Acquired automatically during UPDATE, DELETE, or INSERT. No other transaction can read (with lock) or write that row until the holding transaction commits or rolls back.
  • Shared Locks (S-Locks): Acquired during read operations when explicit locking is requested (LOCK IN SHARE MODE). Multiple transactions can hold shared locks concurrently, but writes are blocked.

Transactions & Concurrency

91. Concurrency Problems

Dirty Reads, Non-repeatable Reads, Phantoms

When multiple transactions execute concurrently without adequate isolation, four classic anomalies can occur:

Problem Description Prevention
Dirty Read A transaction reads uncommitted changes made by another transaction that is later rolled back. READ COMMITTED or higher
Non-repeatable Read Reading the exact same row twice within a transaction yields different values because another transaction modified and committed it. REPEATABLE READ or higher
Phantom Read A query re-executed in a transaction returns newly inserted or deleted rows matching the range filter. SERIALIZABLE / Next-Key Locks
Lost Update Two transactions read the same data and update it concurrently without locking; the second commit overwrites the first. Exclusive locks / Optimistic lock
Transactions & Concurrency

92. Transaction Isolation Levels

SQL-92 Standard Levels & Matrix

The ANSI SQL standard defines four transaction isolation levels offering trade-offs between concurrency throughput and data protection:

Isolation Level Dirty Reads Non-repeatable Reads Phantom Reads
READ UNCOMMITTED Possible Possible Possible
READ COMMITTED Prevented Possible Possible
REPEATABLE READ (MySQL Default) Prevented Prevented Prevented (InnoDB MVCC)
SERIALIZABLE Prevented Prevented Prevented

94. READ COMMITTED Isolation Level

95. REPEATABLE READ Isolation Level

Consistent Snapshots & MVCC

REPEATABLE READ is the default isolation level in MySQL InnoDB. When a transaction starts, its very first read establishes a point-in-time snapshot using Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC). All subsequent queries within that transaction read from this exact snapshot, ensuring consistent, repeatable reads even if other transactions commit modifications.

START TRANSACTION;

-- First read creates MVCC read view:

-- (Session 1 commits update points = 9999)

-- Second read inside Session 2 still returns 500!
SELECT points FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1; -- still 500!

COMMIT;

-- Now after commit, next read sees 9999:

Transactions & Concurrency

96. SERIALIZABLE Isolation Level

Highest Safety & Shared Lock Promotion

SERIALIZABLE is the highest, strictest isolation level. It forces all transactions to execute as if they were serial (one after another). In InnoDB, plain SELECT statements are implicitly converted into SELECT ... LOCK IN SHARE MODE if autocommit = 0, blocking any other transaction from modifying the rows until commit.

Transactions & Concurrency

97. Deadlocks

Deadlock Detection & Resolution

A Deadlock occurs when two or more transactions cannot proceed because each holds a lock that the other needs. Neither transaction can release its lock until it finishes, creating a cyclic dependency. MySQL's InnoDB engine automatically detects deadlocks, chooses a "victim" transaction (the one with the fewest rows altered), rolls it back, and returns Error Code 1213.

Data Types

98. Introduction

Storage Engines & Schema Optimization

Choosing the correct data type for each column is vital for database performance and storage efficiency. Smaller data types consume less RAM in the InnoDB Buffer Pool, allow more index entries per B-Tree page, and accelerate query processing.

Data Types

99. String Types

CHAR vs VARCHAR vs TEXT

MySQL provides specialized string types for different storage characteristics:

  • CHAR(n): Fixed-length strings (0–255 characters). Unused characters are padded with spaces. Ideal for fixed-length data like state codes (CHAR(2)), country codes (CHAR(3)), and postal codes.
  • VARCHAR(n): Variable-length strings (up to 65,535 bytes). Stores only the actual characters plus 1 or 2 length prefix bytes. Ideal for names, emails, and street addresses.
  • TEXT: Used for large text bodies: TINYTEXT (255B), TEXT (64KB), MEDIUMTEXT (16MB), LONGTEXT (4GB). Stored off-page in InnoDB.

Data Types

101. Fixed-point and Floating-point Types

DECIMAL vs FLOAT / DOUBLE

Choosing between exact and approximate numbers is crucial:

  • DECIMAL(p, s) / NUMERIC: Fixed-point, exact precision. p is the precision (total digits, up to 65), and s is the scale (digits after decimal, up to 30). Always use DECIMAL for currency and financial ledgers!
  • FLOAT (4 bytes) & DOUBLE (8 bytes): Floating-point, approximate precision. Store scientific values across huge ranges but are prone to binary rounding errors.

Data Types

103. Enum and Set Types

ENUM vs Lookup Tables

The ENUM type restricts a column to a predefined list of allowed string values (e.g., ENUM('small', 'medium', 'large')). MySQL stores ENUM values internally as 1- or 2-byte integer indexes corresponding to their position in the list.

Pragmatic Advice on ENUMs:

While ENUMs save a small amount of storage, adding or removing a value requires an ALTER TABLE schema change. In production enterprise databases, prefer creating a dedicated lookup table with a foreign key!

Data Types

104. Date and Time Types

DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP

MySQL offers specialized temporal data types:

  • DATE: YYYY-MM-DD ('1000-01-01' to '9999-12-31'). 3 bytes. Ideal for birth dates, invoice dates.
  • TIME: HH:MM:SS (-838:59:59 to 838:59:59). 3 bytes.
  • DATETIME: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS. 5 bytes (+ fractional seconds). Range: 1000 to 9999. Timezone-independent.
  • TIMESTAMP: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS. 4 bytes. Range: 1970-01-01 to 2038-01-19 (Unix epoch). Automatically converted from session timezone to UTC for storage and back.

Data Types

105. Blob Types

Binary Data: Images, PDFs, & Blobs

BLOB (Binary Large Object) types store raw binary data such as images, audio clips, and PDF documents. Variants include TINYBLOB (255B), BLOB (64KB), MEDIUMBLOB (16MB), and LONGBLOB (4GB).

Architecture Warning:

Do NOT store large media files directly in database BLOB columns! It inflates database size, slows backups, and ruins InnoDB Buffer Pool caching. Best practice: Store files on object storage (AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage) and store only the URL string in the database!

Native JSON Storage & Query Operators

MySQL provides native JSON support with automatic validation, efficient binary storage, and JSON query operators:

  • column->'$.path': Extracts a JSON value (retains quotes for strings). Equivalent to JSON_EXTRACT(col, '$.path').
  • column->>'$.path': Extracts a JSON value and unquotes it (clean text). Equivalent to JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(...)).
  • JSON_SET(): Inserts or updates key/value pairs.
  • JSON_REMOVE(): Deletes a key from a JSON object.

Designing Databases

107. Introduction

Architectural Foundations

Database design is the systematic process of structuring data to ensure data integrity, eliminate unnecessary duplication, enforce business rules, and maximize query efficiency. A poorly designed database requires complex, slow queries and easily becomes corrupted with inconsistent data.

Designing Databases

108. Data Modelling

The 4 Sequential Stages

Professional database design follows four sequential stages:

  1. Understand Business Requirements: Interview stakeholders to understand entities, workflows, and business rules.
  2. Conceptual Data Model: Visual representation of high-level business entities and their relationships (without technical details).
  3. Logical Data Model: Detailed schema specifying tables, primary keys, foreign keys, columns, data types, and nullability independent of any specific RDBMS engine.
  4. Physical Data Model: Engine-specific implementation (e.g., MySQL InnoDB), including indexes, collations, storage engines, foreign key action rules, and partitioning.
Designing Databases

109. Conceptual Models

Entities & High-Level Relationships

Conceptual modeling identifies the core business Entities (nouns: Student, Course, Instructor) and the Relationships connecting them (verbs: Student enrolls in Course; Instructor teaches Course). At this stage, technical attributes like data types and foreign key column names are intentionally omitted.

Designing Databases

110. Logical Models

Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERD)

The logical model translates conceptual entities into relational database tables, establishes cardinality (1-to-1, 1-to-Many, Many-to-Many), and defines precise column attributes and constraints.

Designing Databases

111. Physical Models

Engine-Specific Implementation

The physical model tailors the logical model to MySQL's physical storage capabilities, selecting InnoDB, UTF8MB4 collations, primary and secondary B-Tree indexes, and auto-increment strategies.

Designing Databases

112. Primary Keys

Surrogate vs Natural vs Composite

A Primary Key (PK) is a column (or combination of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table. It cannot contain NULL values.

  • Natural Key: An existing real-world attribute that is unique (e.g., Social Security Number, ISBN). Avoid using mutable natural keys as PKs!
  • Surrogate Key: An artificial, system-generated identifier with no business meaning (e.g., AUTO_INCREMENT INT, UUID). Always preferred for stability.
  • Composite Key: A primary key formed from two or more columns (common in link/junction tables).

113. Foreign Keys

Referential Integrity & Relationships

A Foreign Key (FK) is a column in a child table that references the primary key of a parent table. Foreign keys establish relationships and enforce Referential Integrity: preventing child rows from referencing nonexistent parent records.

Designing Databases

114. Foreign Key Constraints

CASCADE, SET NULL, & RESTRICT

When a row in the parent table is updated or deleted, the foreign key constraint determines the action performed on dependent child rows:

  • ON DELETE CASCADE: Automatically deletes all associated child rows when the parent row is deleted.
  • ON DELETE SET NULL: Sets the child foreign key column to NULL when parent is deleted.
  • ON DELETE RESTRICT / NO ACTION: Rejects the delete or update if child rows exist (MySQL default).
  • ON UPDATE CASCADE: Automatically cascades PK changes to child FK columns.

Designing Databases

115. Normalization

Eliminating Redundancy & Anomalies

1. Database Normalization Hierarchy: 1NF to BCNF

Normal FormRequirement & Structural InvariantData Anomalies Eliminated
1NF (First Normal Form)Each column contains atomic (indivisible) values. No repeating groups or arrays. Each row has a unique identifier (Primary Key).Eliminates comma-separated lists and ambiguous row lookups.
2NF (Second Normal Form)Must be in 1NF AND every non-key column must be fully functionally dependent on the entire Primary Key (no partial dependencies on composite PKs).Prevents update anomalies where updating customer name requires updating 50 order items.
3NF (Third Normal Form)Must be in 2NF AND no non-key column may depend on another non-key column (no transitive dependencies: $A o B o C$).Prevents deletion anomalies (e.g. deleting the last employee in a department deletes the department's address).
BCNF (Boyce-Codd NF)Strict 3NF where for every functional dependency $X o Y$, $X$ must be a superkey.Eliminates overlapping candidate key redundancies.

Normalization is the process of organizing data in a database to eliminate redundancy and prevent modification anomalies:

  • Insertion Anomaly: Inability to record certain facts without adding unrelated data (e.g. cannot add a course until a student enrolls in it).
  • Update Anomaly: Inconsistent updates caused by redundant copies of data (updating customer address in 1 order but missing other 5 orders).
  • Deletion Anomaly: Unintended loss of data when deleting a record (deleting the last student enrolled in a course deletes all info about the course itself).
Designing Databases

116. 1NF- First Normal Form

Atomic Values & No Repeating Groups

A table is in First Normal Form (1NF) if:

  1. Each cell contains only a single (atomic) value (no comma-separated lists like 'tag1, tag2, tag3').
  2. There are no repeating groups or columns (e.g., phone1, phone2, phone3).
  3. Every row is uniquely identified by a primary key.

Detailed Practice Problems & Query Analysis

Problem 1: Refactoring Comma-Separated Values into 1NF

Data Deletion
🏢 Business Scenario & Requirement:

Refactor an unnormalized table storing multiple tags per article into 1NF.. In production systems, this query satisfies backend operational workflows while maintaining high throughput and transactional consistency.

Problem1_Query.sql 
-- Unnormalized (Violates 1NF):
-- CREATE TABLE articles_bad (article_id INT, tags VARCHAR(255)); -- 'sql, database, dev'

-- 1NF Normalized Design:
CREATE TABLE articles (
    article_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE article_tags (
    article_id INT NOT NULL,
    tag_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (article_id, tag_name),
    FOREIGN KEY (article_id) REFERENCES articles(article_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

117. Link Tables

Many-to-Many Relationships

Relational databases cannot represent a Many-to-Many (M:N) relationship directly between two tables. An intermediate Link Table (also called a Junction, Associative, or Bridge Table) is created with two foreign keys referencing the two tables, converting the M:N relationship into two 1:Many relationships.

118. 2NF- Second Normal Form

No Partial Functional Dependencies

A table is in Second Normal Form (2NF) if:

  1. It is already in 1NF.
  2. Every non-key column is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key (not just a part of a composite primary key).

If a table has a single-column primary key, it is automatically in 2NF once it satisfies 1NF!

-- Primary Key is (order_id, product_id)
-- quantity depends on BOTH (order_id, product_id) -> Full dependency
-- BUT product_name depends ONLY on product_id! -> Partial dependency!

119. 3NF- Third Normal Form

No Transitive Dependencies

A table is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if:

  1. It is already in 2NF.
  2. It contains no transitive dependencies (a non-key column must not depend on another non-key column).

Famous dictum: "Every non-key attribute must provide a fact about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key, so help me Codd."

120. My Pragmatic Advice

When to Normalize vs Denormalize

Normalize until it hurts, then denormalize until it works:

  • OLTP Systems (Online Transaction Processing): Always normalize to 3NF! Eliminates update anomalies, keeps transactions fast, and ensures data consistency.
  • OLAP / Data Warehouses: Denormalize intentionally (Star schemas, Snowflake schemas) to reduce expensive multi-table joins for analytical aggregations.
Designing Databases

121. Don't Model the Universe

Avoiding Overengineering & YAGNI

A classic design trap is attempting to anticipate every possible future entity or edge case. Model strictly what your software requires today and next quarter. Avoid excessive generic abstractions (e.g. Entity-Attribute-Value antipattern) that ruin performance and developer ergonomics.

Designing Databases

122. Forward Engineering a Model

Visual ERD to Executable DDL Script

In MySQL Workbench, Forward Engineering converts a visual ER diagram directly into a complete SQL DDL script (with CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, and foreign key definitions) and executes it on the database server.

Designing Databases

123. Synchronizing a Model with a Database

Schema Diffing & Migration Script Generation

MySQL Workbench includes a Schema Synchronization wizard that compares your visual model against a live production database, highlights discrepancies, and generates non-destructive ALTER TABLE statements to align them.

Designing Databases

124. Reverse Engineering a Database

Live Schema to Visual ER Diagram

Reverse Engineering connects to an existing database, inspects its schema, foreign keys, and tables, and automatically renders an interactive visual ER diagram in Workbench.

Designing Databases

125. Project- Flight Booking System

Domain Requirements Analysis

Requirements for the airline booking domain:

  • Airports: 3-character IATA code, city, country.
  • Airlines: Code, airline name.
  • Flights: Flight number, departure airport, destination airport, scheduled departure & arrival times.
  • Passengers: First name, last name, passport number.
  • Bookings: Confirmation code, passenger, flight, seat number, booking date, price paid.
Designing Databases

126. Solution- Conceptual Model

Airlines ER Architecture

High-level conceptual entities: Airport, Airline, Flight, Passenger, Booking, and Ticket.

Designing Databases

127. Solution- Logical Model

Complete Normalized Flight Schema

Executable production DDL implementation of the Flight Booking System:

FlightBookingSchema.sql
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS flight_booking_db;
USE flight_booking_db;

CREATE TABLE airports (
    airport_code CHAR(3) PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    city VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    country VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE flights (
    flight_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    flight_number VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    departure_airport CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    arrival_airport CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    departure_time DATETIME NOT NULL,
    arrival_time DATETIME NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (departure_airport) REFERENCES airports(airport_code),
    FOREIGN KEY (arrival_airport) REFERENCES airports(airport_code)
);

CREATE TABLE passengers (
    passenger_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    last_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    passport_number VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE tickets (
    ticket_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    flight_id INT NOT NULL,
    passenger_id INT NOT NULL,
    seat_number VARCHAR(5) NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(8, 2) NOT NULL,

129. Solution- Conceptual Model

Media Rental Architecture

Core entities: Movie, Genre, Customer, Rental, and Payment.

Designing Databases

130. Solution- Logical Model

Complete Normalized Video Rental Schema

Executable production DDL implementation of the Video Rental System:

VideoRentalSchema.sql
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS video_rental_db;
USE video_rental_db;

CREATE TABLE genres (
    genre_id TINYINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE movies (
    movie_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    release_year SMALLINT,
    genre_id TINYINT NOT NULL,
    daily_rental_rate DECIMAL(4, 2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 2.99,
    FOREIGN KEY (genre_id) REFERENCES genres(genre_id)
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    last_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE rentals (
    rental_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT NOT NULL,
    movie_id INT NOT NULL,
    rental_date DATETIME NOT NULL,
    return_date DATETIME NULL,
    rental_fee DECIMAL(5, 2) NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (movie_id) REFERENCES movies(movie_id)
);

DROP DATABASE video_rental_db;

133. Altering Tables

ADD, DROP, MODIFY, & CHANGE Columns

The ALTER TABLE command modifies table structures in existing databases:

  • ADD COLUMN: Appends new column (use FIRST or AFTER col for positioning).
  • DROP COLUMN: Removes a column.
  • MODIFY COLUMN: Changes data type or attributes without changing column name.
  • CHANGE COLUMN: Renames a column and/or updates its type.

134. Creating Relationships

1:1, 1:M, & M:M Relational Schema

Relational databases represent three types of relationships:

  • 1-to-1 (1:1): Foreign key placed in either table with a UNIQUE constraint (e.g. user and user_profile).
  • 1-to-Many (1:M): Foreign key placed in the "Many" child table (e.g. one customer has many orders).
  • Many-to-Many (M:M): Implemented using an intermediate link table with two foreign keys.

Detailed Practice Problems & Query Analysis

Problem 1: Implementing 1-to-1 Relationship with UNIQUE FK

Data Deletion
🏢 Business Scenario & Requirement:

Create a 1:1 relationship between users and profile settings.. In production systems, this query satisfies backend operational workflows while maintaining high throughput and transactional consistency.

Problem1_Query.sql

    user_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE user_settings_1to1 (
    setting_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL UNIQUE, -- UNIQUE guarantees exactly 1:1!
    theme VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'dark',
    FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users_1to1(user_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

136. Character Sets and Collations

utf8mb4 vs utf8mb3 & Unicode Rules

A Character Set is a mapping of characters to binary bytes (e.g., ASCII, Latin1, UTF-8). A Collation is a set of rules for comparing and sorting characters within that set.

Critical MySQL UTF-8 Gotcha:

MySQL's legacy utf8 is actually utf8mb3 (maximum 3 bytes per character) and CANNOT store emojis or certain Asian glyphs. Always use utf8mb4 (up to 4 bytes per character) with default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci in MySQL 8.0+!

Designing Databases

138. A Quick Note

Final Design Architecture Review

Key takeaways for relational database mastery:

  • Use InnoDB exclusively for transactional data integrity.
  • Use utf8mb4 and utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci universally.
  • Surrogate auto-increment integer or UUID primary keys are superior to natural keys.
  • Enforce referential integrity with explicit foreign key naming.
  • Adhere to 3NF for OLTP; denormalize selectively for analytical read performance.
Indexing

139. Introduction

The Power of B-Tree Data Structures

As tables grow into hundreds of thousands or millions of rows, executing a query without an index requires a Full Table Scan (inspecting every single row on disk, O(N) complexity). An Index is an auxiliary B-Tree data structure maintained by the storage engine that allows finding matching rows in logarithmic time (O(log N)), cutting query response times from seconds or minutes to microseconds!

The Trade-off of Indexes:

Indexes accelerate SELECT queries, but slow down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations because every write must also maintain all affected B-Trees on disk. Design indexes purposefully!

Indexing

140. Indexes

Clustered vs Secondary Indexes

1. Physical B+Tree Index Architecture & Node Traversals

In relational databases (MySQL InnoDB), indexes are implemented as balanced multi-way search trees called B+Trees:

Index ComponentStructural CharacteristicsRole in Query Execution
Root NodeTopmost node loaded into RAM Buffer Pool.Starting point for all key search comparisons.
Internal NodesContain key routing boundaries and child pointers; no row data.Directs search traversal down specific tree branches based on key range.
Leaf NodesLowest tier containing actual index entries, arranged as a doubly linked list.Enables extremely fast horizontal range scans (e.g. BETWEEN 10 AND 50) by following sibling pointers without re-traversing the root!
Clustered IndexLeaf nodes store the complete row payload (all columns).Primary key index. The table is the clustered index! Exactly one per table.
Secondary IndexLeaf nodes store the indexed columns + the corresponding Primary Key value.Secondary lookups require a second seek (Bookmark Lookup / Clustered Index Seek) unless covered.
⚠️ SARGability Rule (Search Argument Able): An index seek can only be performed if the indexed column is isolated on one side of the operator without wrapping functions:
• Non-SARGable (Forces Full Table Scan): WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024 — The engine must execute YEAR() on every single row!
• SARGable (Executes Direct B-Tree Seek): WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01' — Direct index range seek!

In MySQL InnoDB, there are two distinct types of indexes:

  • Clustered Index: The actual physical storage organization of the table data itself, ordered by the Primary Key. Leaf nodes contain the full row data. Every table has exactly ONE clustered index.
  • Secondary Index: Any index created on non-PK columns. Leaf nodes store only the indexed column value plus the corresponding row's Primary Key (the bookmark). Secondary index lookups locate the PK, then traverse the clustered index to fetch full row data (unless it's a covering index).

142. Viewing Indexes

SHOW INDEX & Cardinality Statistics

Inspect existing indexes using SHOW INDEX FROM table_name;. Key diagnostic columns include:

  • Non_unique: 0 for unique indexes and primary keys; 1 for non-unique secondary indexes.
  • Key_name: PRIMARY for the clustered PK; custom index name otherwise.
  • Seq_in_index: Column sequence number in composite indexes (1, 2, ...).
  • Cardinality: An estimated count of distinct values in the index. Higher cardinality means higher selectivity!
  • Index_type: Data structure used (almost always BTREE in InnoDB).

143. Prefix Indexes

Optimizing String Indexes & Selectivity

Indexing large VARCHAR or TEXT columns consumes huge amounts of disk space and memory. A Prefix Index indexes only the first N characters of the string (e.g., column(20)). The goal is to choose the smallest prefix length that still provides high Selectivity (the ratio of distinct prefix values to total rows, approaching 1.0).

145. Composite Indexes

Multi-Column Indexes

A Composite Index (also called a compound or multi-column index) indexes multiple columns together in a single B-Tree (up to 16 columns in MySQL). A single composite index on (state, points) is vastly superior to having two separate single-column indexes on state and points because it filters both criteria simultaneously without index merge overhead.

146. Order of Columns in Composite Indexes

Equality First, Range Second & Selectivity

The column order in a composite index dictates which queries can utilize it:

  1. Equality Columns First: Columns queried with exact equality (=) must precede columns queried with ranges (>, <, BETWEEN). Once a range condition is evaluated, subsequent columns in the index cannot be used for filtering!
  2. Higher Cardinality / Selectivity First: Among equality columns, place the column with the highest cardinality first.
Indexing

147. When Indexes are Ignored

SARGable Queries & Index Pitfalls

A query condition is SARGable (Search Argument Able) if the MySQL optimizer can use an index to evaluate it. Common mistakes that cause MySQL to completely ignore indexes:

  • Wrapping Columns in Functions: WHERE YEAR(birth_date) = 1990 (Ignored!) → Rewrite as: WHERE birth_date BETWEEN '1990-01-01' AND '1990-12-31'
  • Arithmetic on Columns: WHERE points + 10 > 1000 → Rewrite as: WHERE points > 990
  • Leading Wildcards: WHERE name LIKE '%son' (B-Tree cannot navigate without prefix)
  • Implicit Type Conversion: Searching a string column with an unquoted integer.

149. Covering Indexes

Zero Clustered Index Bookmark Lookups

A Covering Index is an index that contains all columns requested by a query (in SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY). When a query is covered, MySQL satisfies the request entirely from the B-Tree memory pages without performing any clustered index bookmark lookups to the main table rows. In EXPLAIN, the Extra column displays Using index.

Indexing

150. Index Maintenance

Duplicate, Redundant, & Unused Indexes

Over time, databases accumulate redundant and unused indexes that waste RAM and degrade write performance:

  • Duplicate Indexes: Creating the exact same index twice under different names.
  • Redundant Indexes: An index on (A) is redundant if an index on (A, B) already exists, because (A, B) can satisfy any query on (A) via the leftmost prefix rule!
  • Unused Indexes: Indexes that are never touched by any running query.

Indexing

151. Performance Best Practices

Production Query Optimization Checklist

Golden rules for database index architecture:

  1. Index foreign key columns: Joins on unindexed foreign keys cause Cartesian product scans.
  2. Index columns used in WHERE, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY.
  3. Place equality columns first, range columns second in composite indexes.
  4. Keep indexes narrow: Small column sizes mean more B-Tree keys fit in the InnoDB buffer pool.
  5. Design covering indexes for high-frequency queries.
  6. Never over-index: Regularly audit and purge unused indexes with sys.schema_unused_indexes.
Securing Databases

152. Introduction

Least Privilege & Defense in Depth

Database security protects enterprise data against data breaches, SQL injection, unauthorized modifications, and compliance violations. The foundational doctrine of database administration is the Principle of Least Privilege: every user and application account should be granted only the minimal permissions necessary to perform its intended job, and nothing more.

Securing Databases

153. Creating a User

CREATE USER & Host Restrictions

In MySQL, a user account is identified by both a username and the host/IP address from which they are permitted to connect: 'username'@'hostname'.

  • 'john'@'localhost': Can connect ONLY from the local machine.
  • 'john'@'192.168.1.%': Can connect from any machine on the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet.
  • 'john'@'%': Can connect from any host anywhere in the world (use with extreme caution!).

157. Granting Privileges

GRANT Statements & Permission Hierarchy

Privileges control what actions an account can perform at various levels of granularity:

  1. Global Privileges: *.* (Server-wide, e.g. administrative roles)
  2. Database Privileges: database_name.* (All tables within a schema)
  3. Table Privileges: database_name.table_name (Specific table)
  4. Column Privileges: SELECT (col1, col2) ON table_name (Restricted columns)

159. Revoking Privileges

REVOKE & Least Privilege Enforcement

Privileges are revoked using REVOKE privilege_name ON database.table FROM 'user'@'host';. To remove all privileges simultaneously, use REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES, GRANT OPTION FROM 'user'@'host';.
